facet_selection_reasoning: This selection focuses on the conceptual definition and the center of the sampling distribution, which is the foundational concept for confidence intervals. It specifically tests whether students can distinguish the sampling distribution from the population distribution or a single sample (A3 vs B8, B9) and addresses the misconception that the mean of the sampling distribution changes when the sample size increases (A3 vs B13).

item.stem: The scores on a national certification exam are normally distributed with a population mean $\mu = 500$ and a population standard deviation $\sigma = 100$. A researcher plans to conduct a simulation where they repeatedly take random samples of size $n = 100$ students and calculate the sample mean score $\bar{x}$ for each sample. After thousands of repetitions, they plot the distribution of these sample means. Which of the following correctly describes this sampling distribution?

options.text: The distribution will be centered at $500$ and have a standard deviation of $10$.
options.rationale: This is correct because the mean of the sampling distribution of the mean is equal to the population mean ($\mu_{\bar{x}} = \mu = 500$) and the standard error is $\sigma/\sqrt{n} = 100/\sqrt{100} = 10$.

options.text: The distribution will be centered at $500$ and have a standard deviation of $100$.
options.rationale: A student picking this correctly identifies the mean of the sampling distribution but fails to realize that the sampling distribution is less spread out than the population distribution, incorrectly assuming the standard deviation remains $100$ regardless of sample size.

options.text: The distribution will be centered at $50$ (calculated as $500/\sqrt{100}$) and have a standard deviation of $10$.
options.rationale: This option reflects the misconception that the mean of the sampling distribution depends on the sample size, applying the square root of $n$ adjustment to the mean rather than the standard deviation.

options.text: The distribution is simply the set of $100$ individual scores collected from one specific sample of students.
options.rationale: This choice reveals a confusion between the 'sampling distribution' (the behavior of statistics across many samples) and the 'sample distribution' (the data within a single dataset).

item.explanation: This item tests the properties of the sampling distribution of the sample mean. According to the Central Limit Theorem and the properties of expected values, the mean of the sampling distribution ($\mu_{\bar{x}}$) is always equal to the population mean ($\mu$), regardless of the sample size (addressing A3 and B13). The spread of the sampling distribution (Standard Error) is determined by $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$, meaning it is tighter than the population distribution (addressing B9). Finally, the sampling distribution is a theoretical distribution of a statistic (like $\bar{x}$) over many samples, not the distribution of data points within a single sample (addressing B8).

figures.python_code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import norm

mu = 500
sigma = 100
n = 100
se = sigma / np.sqrt(n)

x = np.linspace(200, 800, 1000)

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4))
plt.plot(x, norm.pdf(x, mu, sigma), 'b-', linewidth=2, label='Population Dist. ($\\sigma=100$)')
plt.plot(x, norm.pdf(x, mu, se), 'r--', linewidth=2, label='Sampling Dist. ($n=100$, $SE=10$)')

plt.title('Comparison of Population and Sampling Distributions')
plt.xlabel('Score')
plt.ylabel('Density')
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
figures.alt_text: A graph comparing a wide normal distribution (population, SD=100) and a very narrow normal distribution (sampling distribution, SE=10), both centered at 500.
